documents.abstract: Large-scale pre-training has improved the generalization of neural operators across diverse PDEs. However, existing PDE foundation models still struggle with heterogeneous dynamics, where shared representations may cause knowledge interference, while mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures suffer from increasing expert redundancy. We propose SPEAR, a spectral-disentangled MoE neural operator with knowledge-guided expert aggregation for large-scale PDE pre-training. SPEAR decouples latent features into low- and high-frequency components, enabling shared modeling of transferable dynamics and specialized learning of PDE-specific patterns. To address expert redundancy, we design a knowledge-guided expert aggregation strategy that measures expert similarity from dataset-specific learned knowledge and routing preferences, enabling the identification and consolidation of similar experts. Experiments on twelve PDE datasets and multiple downstream benchmarks demonstrate superior performance in pre-training, fine-tuning, and transfer learning. Furthermore, our aggregation strategy reduces the number of experts by 50\% while maintaining or improving prediction accuracy, achieving a balance between model efficiency and generalization for PDE foundation models.

Table-to-report generation refers to the task of automatically generating article-level analyt- ical reports from relational tables and is an essential capability for automated data science and decision support. Its central challenge lies in systematically discovering verifiable com- posite insights across tables, attributes, and analytical perspectives, and organizing them into coherent, complete, and traceable evidence chains. Existing methods primarily rely on sequential, reactive data agents or direct Large Language Model(LLM) generation. They suffer from exploration bias: early local observations constrain subsequent actions, causing models to focus prematurely on local analyzes and miss cross-table or cross-dimensional evidence. We propose ComInsight, which reformulates insight discovery as the composition of atomic evidences. We first define an atomic insight as the smallest executable analytical unit conforming to a predefined analysis pattern and enumerate all valid atomic insights from database schema and content. These atoms are then organized into a multi-relational insight graph, where nodes represent verified data facts and edges encode logical, temporal, or hierarchical relations. Finally, a set of composition operators systematically fuses atomic nodes into higher-order composite conclusions. Every composite output is accompanied by executable SQL and fine-grained provenance, ensuring full verifiability. Across three benchmarks InsightBench, DDR-Bench, and T2R-Bench, ComInsight consistently outperforms strong baselines in factual correctness, novelty, and structural completeness. We believe ComInsight offers a reliable, efficient, and explainable path toward table-to-report generation.

Background and context Knowing students’ conceptions of computer science phenomena is essential for the design of teaching–learning settings and instruments. They are particularly interesting in teaching artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) concepts. Therefore, a comprehensive synthesis focused on K–12 is essential to provide educators with actionable conceptions for curriculum design and assessment.Objective We investigate common conceptions of AI/ML in K–12 and to which curricular concepts these can be assigned. We also examine how conceptions vary across age/grade groups and the data collection/evaluation methods employed. This study uniquely synthesizes fragmented research on students’ conceptions of AI/ML into a unified snapshot, offering a systematic mapping that informs curriculum recommendations.Method A systematic literature review according to PRISMA is used to identify the relevant studies. We analyzed the selected literature, extracted the student conceptions, and classified them according to the curricular concepts.Findings We identified 27 relevant studies (from 2007 to 2024) including the conceptions of 1,077 K–12 students from 30 different countries. In addition, our data includes further information on the type of school, age/grade levels, genders and nationalities, the availability of the collected data, and the survey and evaluation methods used. We took a closer look at 29 of the 409 resulting, highly prevalent conceptions, which stand out due to their frequent occurrence.Implications Our findings may be useful for determining in which grade levels interventions targeting specific concepts would be most effective. This could also be used to study the development of these conceptions or developing assessments.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Sustainability has become one of the defining scientific and societal challenges of the twenty-first century. Climate change, rapid urbanization, population growth, increasing energy demand, and declining natural resources require decision-making that is continuous, adaptive, and supported by reliable environmental intelligence. Conventional monitoring systems, which often rely on periodic measurements and isolated analytical tools, are no longer sufficient for managing highly dynamic environmental systems. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), edge computing, and Digital Twins provide unprecedented opportunities to transform sustainability management from reactive monitoring into intelligent, predictive, and autonomous decision-making. IoT enables continuous environmental sensing, AI extracts knowledge from large heterogeneous datasets, edge intelligence supports low-latency analytics, while Digital Twins create dynamic virtual representations of physical systems capable of simulation and optimization. This critical integrative review examines recent developments in AI-enabled sustainability across smart energy systems, intelligent water management, precision agriculture, transportation, smart buildings, circular economy, and climate resilience. Rather than reviewing these technologies independently, the paper analyzes their interactions within an integrated digital ecosystem and discusses emerging topics including Green AI, carbon-aware computing, explainable AI, federated learning, cybersecurity, and sustainability governance. The review method combines a structured multi-database search with targeted evidence and standards updates through June 2026. Building upon the reviewed literature, the paper introduces the Sustainability Intelligence Framework (SIF), a conceptual seven-layer architecture integrating IoT sensing, edge intelligence, AI analytics, Digital Twins, decision intelligence, and sustainability assessment within a continuous feedback cycle. The proposed framework provides a systems-level perspective for designing adaptive, resilient, and resource-efficient infrastructures capable of supporting future sustainable development. The synthesis identifies continuous, auditable sustainability assessment (Layer 7), rather than the underlying six-layer IoT/cyber–physical stack, as the framework’s distinct contribution. It also shows that reported benefits remain difficult to compare because field validation, system boundaries, rebound effects, and lifecycle digital burdens are inconsistently reported.

Recognizing emotion in informal text at the granularity mental health support requires, telling nervousness from fear or remorse from sadness, remains far below usable accuracy: five years of work on Google’s GoEmotions multi-label 28-emotion dataset has reached only .5475 macro F1, and no systematic review has examined why. Accurate emotion recognition is an important predictor of mental healthcare success, yet its subjectivity makes it difficult for even trained human annotators to agree on nuanced emotions in noisy text. Our systematic search identified 494 papers. Inclusion required the full 28-emotion dataset, deep learning models, and reported macro F1, yielding 30 papers and 71 models. Among the highest-scoring models, 9 of the top 10 employ explicit emotion-learning architectures or objective functions. We found no LLM-based models exceeding the foundation paper’s baseline performance. Only 5 of the 71 models underwent extensive hyperparameter tuning. We attributed the observed ceiling to tuning practice as much as architectural limits. Systematic reviews are rare in AI/ML relative to medicine. This scarcity, combined with a submission surge that has outpaced peer-review capacity, plausibly explains why the field’s true state-of-the-art result went unrecognized for years. This recipe book details the emotion-specific design and tuning techniques associated with the strongest results. The strongest results in the corpus are associated with combining explicit emotion-learning architectures, objective functions, and rigorous tuning, though the reviewed models remain well short of the performance likely needed for practical usability in mental healthcare. Current evidence does not support LLMs as a competitive alternative.

Introduction Remote maritime operations increasingly depend on complex, distributed socio-technical systems in which safe and effective performance relies on team cognition rather than on individual decision-making alone. Despite its importance, the conceptualisation and measurement of team cognition in this domain remain fragmented and underdeveloped. Methods A scoping review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Searches of SCOPUS, Web of Science, and EBSCOhost yielded 162 records, of which 51 publications (35 journal articles and 16 conference proceedings, published between 2010 and 2025) were included after screening, retrieval assessment, and expert recommendation. The included publications were thematically analysed using a hybrid deductive-inductive approach. Results Five themes emerged: (1) situation awareness and its measurement and modelling, (2) collective team cognition, learning, and training, (3) human-autonomy teaming and remote collaboration, (4) visualisation and interface design for shared cognition, and (5) maritime applications of distributed cognition. The evidence demonstrates a shift from static, individual-based models toward dynamic, interaction-driven, and system-level accounts, in which team cognition arises from ongoing interactions among human agents, technical artefacts, and environmental constraints. Discussion The findings indicate that shared and distributed situation awareness is central to coordination and safety in remote maritime operations. Key challenges include integrating autonomous systems, designing interfaces that support distributed sensemaking, and reliably measuring team cognition. Enhancing remote maritime safety requires aligning design, training, and regulatory frameworks with the principles of distributed cognition. Future research should prioritise longitudinal and intervention-based validation in real-world operational contexts.

An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure’, said Benjamin Franklin. A Chinese proverb states that ‘inferior doctors aim at a cure of the disease, mediocre doctors treat the impending disease, and superior doctors attempt to prevent the disease’. Safety in healthcare delivery is the prime responsibility of healthcare personnel – preventing errors, reducing both short- and long-term risks, and minimising harm to patients. Modern technology helps in connecting all stakeholders and driving towards preventive care through proactive patient safety measures that can help reduce morbidity and mortality. This is applicable more so in elder care. The population of elderly all over the world is increasing, with a concomitant increase in the percentage of those with chronic diseases. This demographic change and increased longevity are forcing us to re-think traditional reactive healthcare models, specifically in the vulnerable elderly population where technology-enabled, human-centric solutions are required. While technologies for remote monitoring have existed for over two decades and there is growing use of artificial intelligence in healthcare, there is a gap in adoption and pervasive, safe use in senior care. Issues related to the digital divide, lack of standards, inadequate training, and lack of focus on a culture of safety may be preventing progress. We believe, informed by real-world deployment in global senior care settings, especially with reference to India, that healthcare solutions must look at problems comprehensively – going beyond technology – and integrate the preferences and workflows of seniors, care managers, and caregivers for these solutions to be used safely.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Reliable large language models (LLMs) must not only produce accurate answers but also express confidence that faithfully reflects their probability of being correct. Such calibration is essential for identifying uncertain predictions and supporting reliable decision-making in real-world deployment. Recent studies incorporate calibration learning into reinforcement learning (RL), jointly optimizing answer correctness and verbalized confidence using ground-truth correctness supervision. However, their reliance on labeled data limits their applicability in practical test-time settings, where ground-truth labels are unavailable and calibration may need to adapt to newly encountered target tasks. To address this challenge, we propose Test-Time Calibration Learning (TTCL), a label-free framework that jointly adapts reasoning accuracy and verbalized confidence directly on unlabeled target-task data. Specifically, TTCL derives self-supervision signals for both correctness and calibration from multiple model-generated responses, enabling calibration learning at test time without ground-truth labels. Theoretical analysis further establishes TTCL as a bounded surrogate for the ideal calibration objective. Extensive experiments on mathematical reasoning and factual question answering demonstrate that TTCL consistently improves both accuracy and calibration across diverse models and tasks. On base models, TTCL achieves an average relative accuracy improvement of +40.13% and an ECE reduction of +70.80% across eight benchmarks. Moreover, TTCL can further improve both accuracy and calibration for already calibrated models under domain shift, particularly when source-domain calibration transfers poorly to target tasks. In the math-to-factQA setting, TTCL achieves an average relative accuracy gain of +20.35% and reduces ECE by +53.83%. The source code is released at https://github.com/tmlr-group/TTCL.

This report is a continuation of previous efforts to test the ability of large language model (LLM)-driven artificial intelligence (AI) agents to interface with AI-enabled biological tools (BTs). While rapid advancements in BTs in recent years have brought promise to accelerate scientific discovery, they also raise significant biosecurity concerns about potential misuse. The biosecurity community is particularly interested in the extent to which LLMs can lower technical barriers and assist non-expert users in accessing and operating BTs. Despite this interest, few evaluations have focused on LLM-BT interactions in the context of a defined threat model. To address this gap, this report describes a test of frontier LLM-driven AI Agents on their ability to use BTs to redesign peptides and proteins to evade nucleic acid synthesis screening measures. Highly relevant to biorisk, this task assesses a potential capability of AI agents that could enable a breach of a critical early defensive layer designed to prevent a multitude of biological misuse scenarios. The findings presented here intend to offer a foundation for biosecurity researchers and AI developers to conduct or further risk and capability assessments as these technologies progress.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Improving joint audio-visual reasoning in Omni Large Language Models typically incurs substantial data construction and training costs. Our diagnostics reveal multi-hop reasoning difficulties despite correct answers to all corresponding single-hop questions and suggest partial decoupling in the local optimization of perception and reasoning objectives. This motivates post-training with different emphases on these capabilities. Text-only reasoning training yields gains across data sources, model scales, and families. With the best-performing text-only configuration, supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning (RL) raises Qwen2.5-Omni-7B's geometric mean of nine reasoning scores by 25.83% over the base model, outperforming the complete native audio-visual route with 56.6% fewer GPU-hours. Training on data synthesized entirely by a text-only LLM raises this geometric mean by 21.01% without audio-visual data in construction or training. However, text-only training degrades perception. We therefore propose a text-centric post-training paradigm: text-only training provides the main reasoning optimization, and reduced-data native audio-visual RL then refines perception. Refinement uses about 90% fewer input tokens than full-data audio-visual RL, restores perception above the base level, and retains 93.5% of the best-performing text-only pipeline's reasoning gain.

documents.abstract: This chapter delineates the conceptual framework for occupational health and safety (OH&S) performance management, formulated through a comprehensive literature review and a Delphi study incorporating expert insights. The framework incorporates established theories and models such as the ILO-OHS model, Heinrich’s domino theory, Peterson’s multiple causation model, Bird and Germain’s loss causation model, Ferrell’s human factor theory, affective events theory, job demands-resources theory, and Reason’s socio-technical systems approach. These perspectives collectively underscore management commitment, employee engagement, training, hazard identification, continuous improvement, and wellbeing as essential facets of OH&S performance. The framework outlines eight latent constructs: management strategy, finance, employee engagement, training and promotion, hazard identification and review, OH&S culture for continuous improvement, employee wellbeing, and the provision of OH&S services. Each of the constructs is operationalised through quantifiable variables that incorporate established theories and models whose viewpoints contribute to the development of the framework. The framework highlights the interrelationships between organisational leadership, the allocation of resources, and employee engagement as drivers of reducing incidences. This chapter illustrates how the framework provides an organised and easy-to-adopt tool to enhance OH&S performance management practices that are aligned with international standards and best practices and facilitate sustainable workplace safety.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The study addresses the growing challenge of enhancing tertiary students’ Business English writing proficiency in Sri Lanka, where conventional teaching methods often fail to provide sufficient individualized feedback and engagement opportunities. With the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, new opportunities have emerged for personalised, interactive, and feedback-driven writing instruction. Thus, this study investigates the effectiveness of integrating ChatGPT into Business English pedagogy to enhance tertiary students’ writing skills, focusing on the Faculty of Commerce and Management Studies at the University of Kelaniya, Sri Lanka. A mixed-methods design was adopted combining quantitative data from 150 management undergraduates using structured questionnaires, with qualitative data from 10 purposively selected interviewees. Quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS, and qualitative data were examined through thematic analysis. The results indicated strong positive correlation between ChatGPT use and key aspects of Business English writing improvement; personalised feedback (r = 0.915), writing style adaptation (r = 0.887), and writing engagement (r = 0.821), all significant at p < 0.01. Regression analysis further showed that the three ChatGPT-related constructs significantly predicted students’ reported Business English Writing Skills (R² = 0.858, F = 294.336, p < 0.001), with Personalised Feedback (β = 0.713), Writing Style Adaptation (β = 0.478), and Writing Engagement (β = 0.467) making significant positive contributions. Thematic findings supported these results, highlighting enhanced grammar accuracy, vocabulary, coherence, and motivation, alongside reduced writing anxiety. However, challenges such as over-dependence, limited critical evaluation, and risks of academic misconduct were identified. The study recommends that when responsibly integrated, ChatGPT holds substantial potential to enhance Business English writing proficiency and learner engagement in Sri Lankan higher education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study examined the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot counseling and face-to-face counseling on perceived stress, athlete burnout, and resilience among athletes. In this three-arm quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study, 73 athletes participated in AI chatbot counseling, face-to-face counseling, or a control condition over a 12-week intervention period. Nonparametric longitudinal analyses revealed significant group-by-time interactions. After adjustment for multiplicity, significant group-by-time interactions were observed for perceived stress and reduced sense of accomplishment, a sub-variable of athlete burnout. Perceived stress significantly decreased in the face-to-face counseling group, whereas reduced sense of accomplishment significantly decreased in the AI chatbot counseling group. For supportiveness, a sub-variable of resilience, the group-by-time interaction was significant before multiplicity adjustment but did not remain significant after adjustment. These findings indicate different patterns of change across the counseling conditions and psychological outcomes. Given the quasi-experimental design and baseline differences among the groups, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and further investigation is needed to clarify the potential roles of AI chatbot counseling and face-to-face counseling in supporting athletes’ psychological well-being.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT This article analyzes the pedagogical and psychological aspects of the concepts of “independent learning” and “independent work,” which are of great importance in the higher education system. Based on the scientific approaches of international and local scholars, the differences and similarities between these two concepts, as well as their role in the professional development of students, are examined. Keywords: independent learning, independent work, cognitive activity, zone of proximal development, intrinsic motivation, reflection, subject-subject relationship.

Consciousness, on the Four-Model Theory, is constituted by ongoing self-simulation: a system builds a model of itself, relates to that model, and interacts with it. Models divide along two axes — scope (world vs. self) and mode (implicit vs. explicit) — yielding four model kinds rather than four modules. The implicit models are substrate-level, learned, and non-conscious; the explicit models are virtual, transient, and phenomenal. Qualia are constitutive properties of the computational level, incoherent at the substrate level as a spreadsheet cell's value is incoherent at the transistor level, which reframes the Hard Problem as resting on a category error: phenomenal properties are sought at a level where they do not exist. The framework rests on three principles. Open-ended computation allows free modeling, and near-criticality is the signature that property leaves in neural tissue rather than the requirement itself. Recurrent non-linear dynamics of sufficient complexity host a second computational level: persistent activity patterns individuated by their mutual effects rather than by the cells that carry them. Phenomenology is a real, physical effect on that level, arising where the modeling closes on itself — where the self-model and the world-model each enter the other's update rule. That this closure constitutes phenomenality is argued for and not derived (Section 3.4.3). The four kinds are then a minimum the architecture forces rather than a posit: four is the floor, not the ceiling. Redirection of the modeling resource, variable permeability and forking of the self-model follow as consequences, and through them the theory accounts for psychedelic phenomenology, anesthetic mechanisms, dream and lucid-dream states, split-brain phenomena, dissociative identity disorder and animal consciousness. Several claims derived from the theory's 2015 axioms have since received converging independent support (Xu et al., 2024; Hengen & Shew, 2025; Algom & Shriki, 2026), though that convergence concerns the computational requirement and is shared with other criticality-based frameworks. Consciousness, on the Four-Model Theory, is constituted by ongoing self-simulation: a system builds a model of itself, relates to that model, and interacts with it. Natural language generation (NLG) research has focused in the past on mainly two aspects: (i) the process of language generation in itself (e.g., to give theoretical insights into models of human language) and (ii) the use of such approaches to solve applied problems (e.g., generation of medical reports, weather forecasts, etc.). Since the advent of large language models (LLMs), given their "generation capabilities", there has been a tendency among researchers to use LLMs for an increasing number of novel tasks. The use of LLMs raises questions for NLG researchers about which tasks, both theoretical and practical, are still considered NLG tasks per se, and which are still relevant, given that LLMs have solved many former problems in language generation. Through a structured literature search, we investigate domain shift in NLG before and after LLMs and discuss the positive and negative aspects that arise from this, with the aim of providing researchers with greater clarity on where we stand as a field.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative catalyst in Supply Chain Management (SCM), shifting operations from traditional models to predictive and automated systems. This article examines the impact of AI technologies—specifically Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), on supply chain planning. Grounded in Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT) and Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT), we analyze how AI enhances planning efficiency across strategic, tactical, and operational horizons. Furthermore, we critically evaluate key implementation challenges, including data governance, system integration, algorithmic transparency, human-AI trust, and organizational change management. The article concludes with key managerial insights and future research directions for sustainable, resilient, and AI-augmented supply chains.

documents.abstract: The adequate application of artificial intelligence (AI) technology in legal education in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has been barely covered by scholarly literature, especially, from the perspectives of legal and educational sciences. The current paper attempts to fill in an existing gap in literature about the appropriate usage of AI in legal education. The research is intended to help curriculum designers in UAE universities to improve undergraduate legal education programs using innovative AI systems and, thus, to provide UAE policy makers with the academic and ethical standards for the use of AI in legal education. The current paper critically discusses the possible contribution of AI systems in the improvement of the quality of legal education. Moreover, the research analyzes the probable implications of using AI in law curricula for the learning process and for the development of critical legal skills in UAE law students, stressing on the importance of ensuring academic integrity. Furthermore, the current research uses a qualitative approach to analyze the legal, educational, pedagogical, and ethical aspects of AI integration into legal education in the UAE and suggests a legal-pedagogical model of its responsible integration. The goal of the analysis is to determine what opportunities may be offered by AI systems in improving the quality of legal education in the UAE and to discuss their ability to educate students to perform independent legal practice. The discussion focuses on four main areas: (i) the quality of legal education in the UAE’s legal context; (ii) understanding of the AI-enabled legal education systems; (iii) identifying the educational and ethical risks of using AI in legal education; and (iv) setting the standards for the responsible use of AI in legal education. To conclude, the article argues that the adequate use of AI can improve significantly the quality of legal education, if appropriate ethical and academic standards will be developed to ensure the integrity of the process and to develop legal competencies of the students.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This paper is about how the hospitality industry has been changing into a human-centric model through digital technologies and human interactions to create a better customer experience within the Experience Economy. This evolution will focus on providing 'emotional satisfaction' for guests, increasing the level of personalization throughout all aspects of service and creating something new for each individual guest. Additionally, this study will investigate how the combination of 'technology' and 'innovation' will impact current hotel practices to meet the increasing expectations of today's consumers. To this end, qualitative methods were used to gather data from two groups, hotel managers and professionals who specialize in digitization, through interviews to gather information on the role of personalization, artificial intelligence, and interaction of systems on the guest experience in the hospitality industry.

This study analyzes the influence of operational fatigue on airline pilots and copilots operating at a regional airport and its potential impact on aviation safety. Fatigue has been recognized by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) as a critical human factor affecting decision-making, attention, and operational performance in flight operations. The objective of this research is to identify the main factors associated with fatigue among flight crew members and evaluate their relationship with working hours, rest periods, and perceived performance during flight operations. A quantitative, descriptive, and cross-sectional study was conducted using a structured questionnaire applied to airline captains and first officers operating at the local airport. The study population consisted of 112 airline pilots, from which a sample of 41 participants was obtained. Data were collected over a four-week period during operational schedules associated with higher fatigue risk (04:30–06:00 and 22:00–01:00). The survey evaluated variables including working hours, rest periods, sleep quality, fatigue symptoms, and perceived operational performance. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistical methods, including frequency distributions and percentage analysis. The results indicate that a considerable proportion of participants reported symptoms associated with fatigue, including drowsiness, reduced concentration, and decreased alertness during flight operations, particularly during night operations and after extended working hours. Additionally, irregular rest cycles and high operational workload were identified as key factors contributing to fatigue among pilots. The findings highlight the importance of implementing fatigue mitigation strategies and strengthening Fatigue Risk Management Systems (FRMS) within airline operations. This study contributes to the understanding of fatigue as a multidimensional human factor that can influence pilot performance and aviation safety.

Every employment relationship in labour law has, until now, presupposed a visible employer — a person or entity capable of being identified, questioned, and held to account for the direction it exercises over a worker. The gig economy disturbs this premise. Platforms exercise the same functions traditionally associated with an employer — assigning work, setting pay, monitoring performance, and terminating access — not through a visible supervisor but through an algorithm whose rules the worker cannot see and cannot contest. This paper asks whether the traditional control test, built on the assumption of an identifiable, human directing mind, can meaningfully regulate a relationship in which the employer’s authority has become functionally invisible, and if not, how the law should respond. The paper adopts a doctrinal and comparative method. It examines how platforms use ratings, personalised pay, gamification and automated deactivation to manage workers in ride-hailing, delivery and freelance work, and places this alongside the legislative and ballot-driven contest over worker status in California under Assembly Bill 5 and Proposition 22, and the European Union’s 2024 Platform Work Directive, which introduces a rebuttable presumption of employment triggered by defined indicators of algorithmic direction and control. The paper argues that algorithmic management does not eliminate employer control but relocates and conceals it, replacing a visible supervisor with an opaque system that performs the same disciplinary function while evading the doctrinal tests designed to detect it. The paper concludes that the law and workers alike need better tools to hold the invisible employer to account, starting with meaningful access for workers to the criteria used to evaluate and pay them and human review of automated decisions with serious consequences, such as deactivation.

AI is a key driver in the Fourth Industrial Revolution, significantly impacting healthcare. Nursing students’ acceptance and readiness to use AI are crucial for its successful integration. Understanding their perceptions is vital to prepare them for the intelligent healthcare era. To examine the mediation effect of AI anxiety between AI literacy and attitudes towards AI in college nursing students. A cross-sectional study. Nursing students from 10 universities across 7 provinces in China were recruited using convenience sampling from May to June 2025. The data collection tools included the Self-Designed Demographic Questionnaire, the General Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale, the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale and the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale. Data were collated and analyzed using SPSS Statistics 26.0 software and AMOS 29.0 software. The study found that nursing students possess moderate levels of AI literacy and AI anxiety, while generally maintaining positive attitudes towards AI. Mediation analysis indicated that AI anxiety statistically mediated the association between AI literacy and nursing students’ attitudes towards AI. AI literacy was significantly associated with nursing students’ attitudes towards AI, and AI anxiety statistically mediated this association. Therefore, nursing education may benefit from a dual-path approach, designed to simultaneously enhance cognitive competencies (AI literacy) and manage affective responses (AI anxiety).
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing how cancer biology is read, searched, modeled, and turned into hypotheses. But scientific AI does not meet biology directly. Much of what it learns has already passed through English, abstracts, pathway labels, database entries, and text-mined relations. New foundation models create a second translation problem. They can learn from molecular structures, single-cell profiles, perturbation data, and clinical trajectories without first converting those relations into human-readable explanations. This could expand biological and biomedical discovery, but it also changes the burden of proof. If a model proposes a target, biomarker, stratification, or perturbation that is reproducible but only partly interpretable, what evidence should be required before researchers or clinicians act on it? We argue that interpretability is not only an engineering problem. It is a translation problem. When the internal language of a model is difficult to read, the external evidence must become stronger: clear provenance, experimental challenge, cross-population validation, reproducibility, and accountable human judgment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: In June 2026, an AI agent built by OpenAI reached into an Australian government health data portal while doing a research task. By the Prime Minister’s account, it met blocks and found its way around them. The company told the government about three months later. Nvidia has since launched a safety platform that contains agents inside a fixed boundary and stops them in milliseconds if they leave it. That is a useful safeguard. But a boundary can only forbid what someone listed in advance, and an agent that keeps trying after being blocked is showing a pattern, not crossing one line. This note proposes a second layer: a training-free signal that watches how quickly the agent’s own stream of corrections and blocks settles back to normal, with a graded response before any boundary is reached. It is a concept note and has not been tested on real agent logs.

Background Internships connect academic learning with workplace practice, yet the psychological process through which students' academic self-perceptions are associated with internship success remains insufficiently specified. This study examined whether multidimensional internship engagement statistically mediates the association between academic self-concept and internship outcomes. Methods A quantitative, multi-institutional, three-wave time-lagged survey was conducted with 522 undergraduate students from Chinese universities. Academic self-concept was assessed at internship entry, internship engagement at the internship midpoint, and internship outcomes after completion. Established instruments were adapted through forward translation, back-translation, expert review, and pilot testing. Confirmatory factor analysis, latent-variable structural equation modeling, 5,000-resample bootstrap mediation analysis, full-information maximum likelihood, robustness checks, and subgroup analyses were used. Results The hypothesized three-factor measurement model fit better than the two-factor and one-factor alternatives. The structural model showed acceptable fit (CFI = 0.958, TLI = 0.953, RMSEA = 0.034, and SRMR = 0.044). Academic self-concept was positively associated with internship engagement, and internship engagement was positively associated with internship outcomes. The indirect association through internship engagement was 0.249 (95% bootstrap confidence interval: 0.184 to 0.319). The proportion mediated was 50.6% (95% bootstrap confidence interval: 39.4% to 62.6%), and the direct association remained statistically significant. The pattern was stable across alternative specifications and exploratory subgroup analyses. Conclusion Internship engagement statistically accounted for part of the association between academic self-concept and internship outcomes. The findings support a theoretically ordered, but not causal, pathway in which students' academic self-evaluations are associated with stronger behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement during workplace learning.

Preoperative optimization clinics enhance surgical outcomes by optimizing patients' health, reducing unnecessary tests, and minimizing cancellations. Artificial intelligence (AI) now promises to further advance these efforts by improving predictive modeling, automating risk assessments, and enabling personalized care strategies. AI models have shown particular strength in predicting postoperative complications, such as cardiovascular events. Tools like natural language processing (NLP) have also improved risk detection for conditions like alcohol misuse. The historical development of preoperative clinics-from Dr. J Alfred Lee's initial concept in 1949 to modern models like Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) and Anesthesia Preoperative Evaluation Clinic (APEC)-laid the groundwork for today's integration of electronic health records (EHRs) and decision-support systems, now evolving toward AI-driven care. Machine-learning algorithms have proven superior to traditional models for predicting postoperative anemia, opioid dependence, diabetes complications, and mortality risks, thus offering precise stratification and resource optimization. Specific applications include AI-assisted anemia management, penicillin allergy delabelling, and opioid use prediction after major surgeries. AI also enhances patient education through tools like ChatGPT and improves smoking cessation efforts using conversational AI. NLP has demonstrated better accuracy than standard International Classification of Disease (ICD) codes in identifying risky alcohol use (>2 standard drinks per day before surgery). However, barriers to widespread adoption include data privacy, algorithmic bias, and clinician skepticism. Future studies should focus on validating AI models across diverse populations and integrating AI recommendations within clinical workflows while adhering to evolving regulatory standards. Ultimately, AI's incorporation into preoperative assessments could significantly boost the efficiency and impact of clinic resources, potentially shifting outcomes more favorably by improving the slope of resource utilization versus patient outcome curves. Continued research and refinement are essential for AI to achieve its full potential in perioperative medicine.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Cancer, Stress, Anesthesia, and Immune Response

documents.abstract: Remote work has become one of the most consequential and contested organizational changes of the modern workplace. Yet discussions about remote and hybrid work are often reduced to a binary disagreement between advocates of employee flexibility and leaders who prioritize office attendance. This working paper argues that the central question is not whether remote work universally succeeds or fails. The more useful question is which combinations of tasks, employees, managerial practices, communication systems, performance measures, and workplace arrangements allow remote work to produce sustainable value. The paper presents a practitioner-led narrative review of influential field experiments, observational studies, meta-analytic research, and international institutional evidence concerning remote and hybrid work. It examines six major outcome areas: employee productivity, retention, collaboration, professional learning, well-being, and equitable access to opportunity. The evidence indicates that the effects of remote work are heterogeneous rather than universally positive or negative.Research reviewed in the paper shows that remote work can increase measured performance in structured roles with observable outputs, limited task interdependence, and suitable working conditions. Hybrid arrangements can improve employee satisfaction and materially reduce voluntary turnover without reducing performance. Location flexibility can also broaden access to talent, reduce commuting burdens, support caregivers, and enable organizations to recruit beyond their immediate geographic markets. However, remote work can create important organizational costs when it is introduced without an appropriate operating system. Large-scale evidence suggests that firm-wide remote work can make collaboration networks more static and siloed, shift communication toward asynchronous channels, and reduce opportunities for spontaneous cross-team interaction. Distance can also weaken informal mentoring, slow the development of early-career employees, increase coordination costs, blur boundaries between professional and personal life, and expose weaknesses in management that physical proximity previously concealed.To reconcile these competing outcomes, the paper introduces the “remote work paradox”: the same flexibility that improves autonomy, retention, and focused individual work can simultaneously weaken collaboration, shared context, informal learning, and organizational connection. These effects are not mutually exclusive. A company may experience lower employee turnover while its internal collaboration network becomes narrower. An employee may complete more individual tasks while receiving less coaching and having fewer opportunities to form professionally valuable relationships. The paper proposes the REMOTE operating framework as a practical approach for designing and evaluating distributed work. The six dimensions of the framework are Role suitability, Expectation clarity, Managerial cadence, Output evidence, Team connection, and Equitable access. Together, these dimensions reposition remote work as an organizational-design challenge rather than a debate about employee location.Role suitability requires organizations to examine the actual tasks within each position and determine which activities benefit from quiet concentration, which require physical resources, and which depend on rapid coordination or tacit knowledge. Expectation clarity requires written outcomes, ownership, deadlines, quality standards, communication norms, and escalation procedures. Managerial cadence concerns the predictable systems through which managers provide coaching, feedback, prioritization, and workload review. Output evidence requires performance to be assessed through meaningful results rather than online visibility or digital activity. Team connection addresses trust, mentoring, weak ties, shared context, and cross-functional collaboration. Equitable access requires organizations to ensure that remote employees receive fair access to information, important assignments, feedback, sponsorship, compensation, and promotion opportunities. The paper also develops seven propositions that organizations can evaluate using their own operational data. These propositions address task suitability, coordinated hybrid schedules, employee retention, differences between experienced and early-career workers, the value of documentation, the influence of managerial capability, and the risk of proximity bias. The propositions are not presented as newly established causal findings. Instead, they translate the reviewed literature into testable expectations that organizations can use when conducting workplace-policy pilots. A five-stage implementation protocol is presented for employers. Organizations are encouraged to diagnose their work processes, design an explicit location model, pilot the model for a defined period, measure a balanced set of outcomes, and adapt the policy according to the evidence. Recommended measurements include productivity, work quality, cycle time, employee turnover, absenteeism, customer outcomes, collaboration patterns, onboarding progress, feedback latency, workload, employee experience, and equity across demographic and location groups. The paper concludes that remote work should be understood as an organizational technology whose value depends on complementary investments in management, documentation, communication, cybersecurity, job design, performance measurement, and inclusive employment practices. The strongest remote-work policy is neither the most permissive nor the most restrictive. It is the policy that makes productive work easier, learning faster, accountability clearer, collaboration more intentional, and professional opportunity more equitable.
topics: Personal Information Management and User Behavior

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly incorporated into digital media and more generally into production workflows with which the public frequently interacts. Current provenance standards and disclosure methods frequently rely on binary categorizations, differentiating only between entirely human-authored and AI-generated content, or depend on technical watermarking that lacks user-facing clarity. However, there are very different risks and outcomes depending on the different uses of AI in the creation and consumption of end products. Therefore, we propose the Reported Engagement with AI Level (REAL) Rating framework which addresses these concerns by introducing a six-tier scale (Levels 0-5) that discloses the extent of AI involvement in both product creation and user experience. This paper details the structural methodology of the REAL Rating system and the specifics of its application across text, image, audio, video, and software products.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The role of artificial intelligence (AI) in transforming financial accounting and tax compliance is one of those areas that have become very intricate in terms of regulation. Based on the systematic review and synthesis of recent empirical research and industry surveys (2021–2026), the study evaluates how AI, including machine learning, natural language processing, and generative AI, transforms essential accounting and tax processes. As follows, the implementation of AI technologies leads to efficiency gains, including 81% productivity increases and the enhancement of accuracy up to 98%. Companies using AI-powered compliance solutions attain the accuracy rate in fraud detection of more than 98%, while the processing time is reduced to less than a second. However, despite numerous benefits, there are still some challenges identified, including the lack of appropriate internal skills among 44% of respondents and low data readiness among 80% of respondents. Thus, the paper concludes that effective application of AI technologies is possible only through effective collaboration between humans and AI and appropriate governance, which requires significant investments into data infrastructure.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Hospitals present various occupational hazards, making the implementation of Hospital Occupational Health and Safety (OHS/K3RS) essential to protect all workers, including non-medical staff. This study aimed to analyze the role of hospital management in improving compliance with the OHS program among non-medical staff at the West Java Provincial Occupational Health Regional Hospital. A descriptive qualitative design was used with six informants selected through purposive sampling. The findings showed that management played an important role through the establishment of K3RS policies and the K3RS Team, confirmed by 50% of informants; provision of personal protective equipment (PPE) and OHS training, confirmed by 83.3%; and periodic program monitoring and evaluation, confirmed by 50%. Compliance among non-medical staff was generally good in PPE use, adherence to standard operating procedures, and participation in OHS activities, each confirmed by 50% of informants, although 66.7% reported variation in compliance across work units. All informants (100%) identified management commitment, policies, PPE, training, and unit-head support as enabling factors, while 66.7% reported barriers including budget limitations, limited K3RS human resources, PPE availability, workload, and inconsistent worker awareness. Management commitment therefore emerged as a key determinant, indicating the need to strengthen monitoring, OHS facilities, continuous training, and safety culture to sustain compliance.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The moral and legal case for reparations for transatlantic chattel slavery has advanced far ahead of any credible mechanism for paying them. Quantifications such as the 2023 Brattle Group report place the global liability at USD 100-131 trillion, with tens of trillions attributed to Britain alone - sums that no state can meet from general taxation. This paper proposes a funding mechanism that does not draw on the general taxpayer: a small ad valorem levy (3-5 per cent) on commercial artificial-intelligence inference - the sale of machine-generated "tokens" - collected at the billing layer of cloud and model-API providers, ring-fenced in statute, and securitised through the issue of long-dated sovereign Reparation Bonds. The mechanism deliberately mirrors, in reverse, the instrument through which Britain financed the GBP 20 million compensation paid to slave owners under the Slavery Abolition Act 1833: a debt serviced from general taxation across generations, whose successor instruments were not redeemed until February 2015, so that descendants of the enslaved were themselves among the taxpayers who serviced it. We model three revenue scenarios against current market data and show that the levy could realistically service USD 40 billion to USD 1 trillion of reparations bonds over the coming decade, scaling automatically with the growth of the AI economy. We position the proposal against the emerging token-tax literature and argue that its contribution is the ring-fencing of AI-derived fiscal capacity to a specific historical liability: the unpaid labour debt of slavery, settled by the automated labour that now substitutes for human work. The mechanism is presented as a credible first instalment and a scalable architecture, not a full settlement. Note on version 6 (October 2026): this version corrects the United Kingdom liability figure given in earlier versions, which was a sterling conversion of a single scenario in the Brattle report presented as the report's own figure, and removes a levy rate attributed to a named executive that could not be verified against a primary source. It also adds sections on the 1833 parliamentary debates and on Jamaica's 2026 petition to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The corrections are set out in full in the "Note on this version" section at the front of the paper.

Issues concerning the relationship between productivity and wages are directly linked to attempts to assess the outcomes of human labor. As the intellectual component of labor increases and the share of services grows, the challenge of quantifying labor becomes increasingly acute. This article examines the evolution of theoretical approaches to understanding productivity and wages — from the mercantilists and the classical school to the new neoclassical synthesis. The study reveals a trend toward an increasing role of the human factor and greater attention to intrinsic motivation when examining the relationship between labor productivity and wages. The contemporary understanding of the productivity–wage nexus is gradually moving away from purely market-based concepts toward incorporating the socio-psychological dimensions of labor relations. The findings may be used to develop recommendations for improving the remuneration system in the Russian Federation.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: The field of Occupational Health and Safety (OH&S) is multidisciplinary in nature and crosscuts sectors, ensuring the safety and health of workers, including their well-being, to improve productivity through the identification and control of hazards at workplweaces. The theoretical and conceptual perspectives of OH&S have been explored in this chapter, stressing the responses to global catastrophic accidents and the effect of globalisation on OH&S and illustrating definitions advanced by various institutions and scholars. Significant to OH&S, the chapter highlights the integration of occupational health, safety management systems, and risk management practices to enhance safe workplaces and organisational culture positively. The discussions delve deeper into accident causation theories, such as Heinrich’s work and succeeding theories that attribute accidents to unsafe conditions, human error, organisational factors, and random events. The cost of accidents through economic, social, and moral perspective is analysed, differentiating direct and indirect impacts on workers, employers, and the communities. Further, tangible and intangible benefits of investing in OH&S have been shown to enhance effective management and lessen accident occurrence, enhance employee well-being, and improve the reputation of an organisation while adding to sustainable competitiveness. In essence, OH&S is outlined to be a human-centric and technical field fundamental to a more resilient and progressive firm and society.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Time series forecasting (TSF) increasingly drives decisions in transportation, energy, finance, healthcare, and infrastructure, yet current evaluation remains overly narrow: standard benchmarks reward low held-out error, while robustness studies typically reduce failure to Gaussian noise, random masking, or bounded adversarial perturbations. This obscures the real failure modes of deployed forecasting systems. Input-side anomalies are not merely noisier inputs: they often reflect structured events that alter temporal dynamics, break cross-variable dependencies, induce regime shifts, or propagate from faulty sensors to downstream decisions. These semantic, causal, and system-level failures cannot be faithfully captured by i.i.d. perturbations alone. The rise of TSF foundation models makes this evaluation gap more urgent, as unauditable pretraining corpora make held-out generalization increasingly unreliable. We therefore advocate scenario-grounded stress testing. Each test instance should include historical inputs and future targets, together with a semantic scenario, an explicit failure operator, and a measurable difficulty level. This shift makes evaluation interpretable, attributable, and deployment-relevant and friendly, enabling the community to ask not only which model is accurate, but under what conditions it fails and why.

Tool-equipped AI agents use tool calls to access data and act on external systems. Horizontal growth of agentic systems increases the number of these interactions, and further motivates the need for automated, per-call oversight that can operate at low latency and/or on-prem. Conventional authorization schemes can determine whether an agent is allowed to invoke a tool, but cannot assess the agent's underlying cognition, specifically, whether the tool selection represents a logical, relevant step toward satisfying the intent of the task or not. Consequently, an allowed call may still deviate from the task's intent: a rogue agent might deviate the calls or nudge other agents to make a combination of calls that would not align with the intent of the task. Therefore, every call needs to be verified. In this study we investigate the applicability of Small Language Models (SLMs) to this purpose: an SLM functions as a task-tool relevance classifier that evaluates every selected tool independently against the assigned task and returns a relevance signal for downstream enforcement. Equipped with a novel dataset with multi-tool tasks whose required tools span distinct Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, we used prompt-optimization, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning through GRPO to optimize and specialize SLMs.

In this article, we examine ten traffic‑themed boardgames published in Finland between the 1950s and 1970s. We introduce our novel concept of played mobilities as an analytical category of imagined mobilities. The concept of played mobilities refers to the active and performative manners of imagining traffic within a framework suggested by any game but also to the potential ways a player can stretch and break a game’s established rules. Our study demonstrates how traffic games were specifically used to teach children and young people about how to behave within a traffic system that was primarily dictated by automobility. These games’ introduction was driven by an increase in the number of cars, changes in traffic regulations, and the rise in traffic accidents in Finland. However, these games also inspired an understanding of traffic as something playable and a highly individualist notion of participating in traffic. During the 1970s, the games increasingly acknowledged other forms of mobility as well. At the same time, their depictions of traffic shifted from futuristic sociotechnical imaginaries towards more realistic traffic scenarios and environments as the car-centric traffic system had, by then, transformed into a mundane aspect of everyday life for most Finns.

LLM agents for clinical text-to-SQL applications reason autonomously over multiple steps but cannot assess whether their own reasoning or outputs can be trusted. In high leverage applications such as healthcare, this presents a critical risk where system mistakes can be costly. These reliability failures are also resource failures: an incorrect reasoning trajectory spends computation budget on outputs that must be discarded. We introduce Sentinel, a trajectory-derived, classifier-based confidence layer that analyzes an agent's reasoning, code and database outputs to decide at three points whether to stop: refusing unanswerable questions before the agent runs, halting doomed trajectories mid-run, and withholding untrustworthy answers at delivery. Here, utilizing Chow's rule, we optimize decisions under the EHRSQL shared task's Reliability Score, which penalizes incorrect answers given a utility weighting, and find on the benchmark EHRSQL that Sentinel raises this score from +0.08 to +0.24 when mistakes have a low utility weighting, well above the +0.03 earned by refusing every question, with delivered-answer accuracy rising from 54% to 69% as coverage falls from 84% to 55%. At higher stakes the agents we test rarely answer reliably enough to deliver, and Sentinel detects this on its own, abstaining to that same +0.03 where the unmonitored agent scores -3.02. The same stopping decisions cut computation: at low stakes, where the system still answers, Sentinel eliminates 13-28% of agent steps at little or no reliability cost.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Aim: This study aims to analyze the development of digital transformation in financial accounting, identify dominant technologies and research themes, and explore research gaps in the field of digital transformation in financial accounting. Method: This study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 framework. The data consist of scientific articles obtained from Scopus, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Emerald Insight, Google Scholar, and other scholarly sources. A total of 18 articles published between 2017 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed using content analysis with a thematic analysis approach. Results: The findings indicate that blockchain is the most dominant technology in the transformation of financial accounting due to its contribution to transparency, accountability, financial reporting quality, and fraud mitigation. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and automation also play important roles in improving the efficiency of accounting and auditing processes and supporting data-driven decision-making. However, existing research remains largely dominated by conceptual and literature-based studies, while empirical research examining the implementation of digital technologies in accounting practices remains relatively limited. Conclusion/Novelty/Implications: The novelty of this study lies in systematically mapping dominant technologies and research themes while identifying empirical research gaps. The findings imply that future research should integrate technology, governance, regulation, cybersecurity, and human resource competencies to support effective and sustainable digital transformation in financial accounting.
topics: Legal and Policy Analysis in Indonesia

documents.abstract: In the Industrial Revolution 4.0 era, the limitation of conventional marketing reach and low adoption of digital technology pose major challenges to cooperative sustainability. Koperasi Serba Usaha (KSU) Rakyat Sejahtera Abadi (Raja) Bekasi possesses strong asset potential of IDR 2.5 billion with 450 active members. However, the cooperative faces stagnant member growth (<5% annually) with 70% of members aged over 45, primarily due to 100% reliance on conventional marketing strategies (zero digital content). This Community Service (PkM) project aims to boost the digital capacity of cooperative managers and members through training in business social media account setup, digital target audience mapping, and short video content creation on TikTok integrated with Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. The execution methods consisted of preparation (assessment), implementation (lectures, discussions, and hands-on practical guidance), and evaluation. Held on April 19, 2026, in Rawalumbu, Bekasi City, the event engaged 60 participants. The results demonstrated a significant enhancement in participants' hard skills regarding storyboard creation, promotional video production for savings and loan products, and TikTok algorithm optimization. This initiative successfully laid a sustainable digital transformation foundation for KSU Raja to expand market reach and attract younger generation.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: In the AI era, trust, ethics, and brand reputation converge in governance, making them inseparable. This chapter examines that claim through four cases: the UAE's state-led AI strategy, the EU's rights-based regulatory model, and the contrasting trajectories of Anthropic and OpenAI. It argues that reputational credibility in AI depends less on innovation narratives or ethical branding than on whether ethical claims rest on visible, contestable, and durable institutional arrangements. To clarify this, it proposes a reputational architecture of trust built on structural, relational, and procedural dimensions. It also shows how governance quality reaches consumers through media coverage, recourse mechanisms, reviews, trust marks, and employee word of mouth. The chapter concludes that governance is not a compliance add-on but a central condition of legitimate innovation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: At the close of the twentieth century, human semantic memory was thought to be organized around dedicated, domain-specific modules operating independently of one another and of perception, action, and much of language. The intervening years have marked a transition toward a more holistic view in which semantics emerges from learned mappings among sensory, motor, and language representations, with recent work beginning to integrate semantic representation with theories of cognitive control and attention. This article reviews the reasons for this remarkable change in perspective, provides a snapshot of our current understanding of semantics in the mind and brain, and considers how this understanding may change in light of new innovations in artificial intelligence.

his article presents Historical Structuralism as an educational framework designed to integrate universal curricular knowledge through a base-10 logarithmic matrix of time and space, from the Big Bang to the present. Grounded in Big History, the model aims to foster intrinsic motivation by making knowledge meaningful and personally significant for learners. A field study was conducted at Mexico’s National Museum of Anthropology with a family of indigenous descent, using a guided tour structured around three didactic charts and a post-visit Likert-scale questionnaire. Results showed that 92.6% of responses concentrated in the highest positive categories (Totally and Quite a bit), with no responses indicating apathy or rejection. Qualitative observations revealed strong emotional engagement and recognition of historical identity. The study offers empirical evidence that Historical Structuralism, when applied in historical museum settings, transforms the museum experience into a catalyst for cognitive and affective connection with universal history.

Environmental sustainability in the hospitality sector increasingly depends on the alignment between employees’ intrinsic motivations, supportive organizational contexts, and environmentally responsible behaviors. Drawing on SelfDetermination Theory, this study examines how Harmonious Green Passion influences environmental performance in Egypt’s five-star hotels, focusing on the mediating role of pro-environmental behavior and the moderating effect of green organizational climate. Data were collected through a cross-sectional survey of 402 hotel employees and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling. The findings demonstrate that Harmonious Green Passion positively influences both proenvironmental behavior and environmental performance, while pro-environmental behavior partially mediates the relationship between Harmonious Green Passion and environmental performance. Furthermore, green organizational climate significantly strengthens the positive relationship between Harmonious Green Passion and pro-environmental behavior, consequently reinforcing its indirect effect on environmental performance. These findings extend Self-Determination Theory by elucidating a motivation–behavior–performance mechanism through which employees’ environmentally oriented passion translates into organizational outcomes, while demonstrating that this process is contingent upon contextual organizational conditions. Practically, the findings suggest that hotel managers should cultivate supportive green organizational climates, encourage employees’ intrinsic environmental motivation, and facilitate pro-environmental behaviors through appropriate organizational practices. Such efforts can strengthen employees’ environmental engagement and contribute to improved environmental performance, offering hospitality organizations a pathway toward more sustainable operations and long-term environmental value creation.

The swift convergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), online instruction, and mobile dependence has transformed higher education, introducing both innovations and ethical problems for allied health training. Although individual studies on AI adoption, digital ethics, and device dependence exist, a significant empirical gap remains regarding how psychological reliance on mobile devices (nomophobia) and virtual-specific ethics jointly drive GenAI adoption among healthcare students, where ethical lapses directly impact clinical competence. To address this gap, this study examined the predictive roles of academic integrity, online learning integrity, and nomophobia in the use of AI tools among allied healthcare students at a higher education institution. Employing a quantitative cross-sectional design, the researchers collected data via convenience sampling among 300 full-time allied health students in Central Luzon, Philippines. The study used four research tools to gather pertinent data for the investigation, including an online survey administered during the second semester of the 2025-2026 academic year. Both descriptive and inferential statistics were employed using SPSS 23. Descriptive results showed high academic integrity, moderate AI usage and nomophobia, but low online learning integrity. Correlation analyses showed that AI tool use was positively associated with online learning integrity, nomophobia, and academic integrity. Multiple linear regression demonstrated that the model significantly predicted AI usage. Online learning integrity was the strongest predictor, followed by academic integrity and nomophobia. These results show that ethical digital engagement and mobile connectedness actively propel AI integration; ultimately, achieving SDG 4 objectives within healthcare education requires moving beyond prohibitive policies toward anticipatory digital governance, robust AI literacy, and ethical models that prepare future professionals for a digitally driven medical environment.

Conditionally automated vehicles still require drivers to retake control when automation reaches its operational limits, so takeover request (TOR) design remains a safety concern. This study developed and evaluated a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system that uses a large language model (LLM) to produce parameter-specific, literature-grounded TOR plans. Two literature corpora on takeover factors and alert modality served as the knowledge base, and a structured situation object represented driver traits, driver state, non-driving-related tasks, and driving scenario conditions. The system generated TOR plans across 10 parameter categories for 40 persona-scenario combinations. Several TOR parameters varied with takeover-relevant inputs in the generated test set, and modality recommendations changed according to the sensory impairments described in the situation object. These preliminary results suggest that RAG-based LLMs may support parameter-specific TOR personalization in automated driving.

This exploratory study examined the relationship between the massage modalities used, the length of the massage treatment, and the areas of the body massaged on the perceived self-reported effort level and muscular fatigue as well as the ergonomic sensor data for average composite risk score and average fatigue risk score. Participants completed their normal routine of massages while wearing sensors: watch placed on the upper arm to collect physiological data; GoX ® sensor placed on the dominant upper arm and back of the shirt to collect ergonomic data. Participants performed massages in their regular clinic, following their normal treatment plan. Following each session, a survey was completed about the massage treatment, including areas massaged, techniques used and self-reported effort and muscle fatigue. Mean self-reported effort level was 10.71± 2.40, light level on the Borg Scale. Mean self-reported muscular fatigue level was 2.69 ± 0.75, light activity on the RPE scale. Length of time of the massage session was not a strong indicator of subjective or objective measures. No one technique provided an increased risk of fatigue. This exploratory study gave a snapshot into fatigue and risks for work-related musculoskeletal disorders in massage therapists while practicing in their normal clinical setting.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces
